title: Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia
text: Completed · manuscript in preparation

title: Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia
text:
Research question
How much cropland is there in North Africa’s main cereal-producing regions, and how well do satellite cropland products represent it?

title: Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia
text:
Scientific motivation
Satellite cropland products differ both in how much cropland they map and in what they count as cropland. In North Africa, agricultural area is known mainly from such products and from administrative statistics. Independent, probability-based reference data are scarce.

title: Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia
text:
Geographic scope
Principal cereal-producing regions of Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia. The survey domains cover 12.44, 12.88 and 3.32 Mha respectively. Cereal reference season: September 2023 to July 2024.

title: Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia
text:
Data and methods

Sampling design. A stratified two-stage probability design, using identical rules in each country. 15 primary sampling units (PSUs) were drawn per stratum (high, medium and low agricultural density), giving 45 PSUs per country. 10 secondary sampling units were drawn per PSU, giving 450 observations per country and 1,350 in total. WorldCereal was used only to build the sampling frame and strata.
Field campaigns. Morocco, February–March 2024. Algeria, March–June 2024 (two campaigns). Tunisia, April–May 2024. Each observation was assigned to one of 18 agricultural and land-cover classes.
Estimation and assessment. Design-based estimators for cereal and cropland area. Accuracy assessment of three public products: GLAD annual cropland, Esri–Impact Observatory land cover, and GACED30.




Sampling design: stratified sampling domain, a selected primary sampling unit, and a field reference observation.

title: Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia
text:
Principal findings

Cropland area. Under a harmonized definition (active herbaceous crops, fallow and tilled land, excluding woody-only agriculture), estimated cropland was 7.015 Mha in Morocco, 6.786 Mha in Algeria and 2.028 Mha in Tunisia. Fallow made up 31.7% of cropland.
Product differences. Relative to these estimates, GLAD mapped 20.5%, 21.3% and 14.4% less cropland (Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia). Esri–Impact Observatory mapped 33.4%, 45.1% and 33.0% less. GACED30 mapped 11.2%, 0.7% and 15.2% more.
Fallow. Disagreement was concentrated in fallow. GLAD, Esri–Impact Observatory and GACED30 classified 50.2%, 33.6% and 74.4% of fallow observations as cropland, against 85.8%, 66.7% and 91.9% of active herbaceous observations.
Definitions. Adding woody agriculture (olive, citrus, orchards) to the reference definition, to match GACED30, reversed the direction of its area difference in all three countries (6.8%, 7.1% and 12.2% less).




Field photographs from the 2024 campaign, paired with Sentinel-2 imagery, showing the agricultural states recorded on the ground.

title: Cropland Mapping and Area Estimation in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia
text:
Scientific significance
Disagreement between satellite products and agricultural-area estimates can come from incomplete representation of agricultural land, from differences in what counts as cropland, or from both. Probability-based reference data that keep each observation’s agricultural state make it possible to separate these sources and estimate area with quantified uncertainty. The survey needed about US$10,000 per country in direct campaign costs, a scale within reach of national agricultural services.

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance
text: Accepted · Environmental Research: Climate

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance
text:
Research question
When does drought become a matter of institutional concern, and how is that recognition related to drought conditions over cropland?

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance
text:
Scientific motivation
In drylands, formal impact records are often incomplete. Climate risk emerges from the interaction of rainfall deficits, agricultural dependence, public concern and governance response. Across North Africa, governments periodically organize Islamic rain rituals (Ṣalāt al-Istisqāʾ) in response to water scarcity. Their announcements leave a public record of when drought becomes institutionally recognized.

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance
text:
Geographic scope
Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia, 2000–2024.

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance
text:
Data and methods

Event record. 63 state-organized Rain Ritual Events (RREs), compiled through longitudinal archival content analysis. Microfilmed national newspapers (El Moujahid, Le Temps, Al Bayane) at the U.S. Library of Congress were reviewed for 2000–2015, and digital archives, press agencies and ministry platforms for 2015–2024.
Drought over cropland. SPEI at 1-, 3-, 6- and 12-month accumulation periods, computed from CHIRPS v3 precipitation and CHIRTS temperature, with FAO Penman–Monteith evapotranspiration from ERA5-Land inputs. Restricted to cropland and aggregated nationally and within sub-national drought clusters.
Analysis. Logistic regression linking the odds of an RRE to drought severity.





Newspaper archives reviewed to build the event record.





A microfilm reel from the national newspaper collection.

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance
text:
Principal findings

The odds of an RRE rose as drought over cropland intensified.
All RREs occurred within the rainfed cropping season, and more than two-thirds between November and February.
The best-fitting drought timescale differed by country: one-month SPEI in Algeria, three-month SPEI in Tunisia, and one-, three- and six-month SPEI about equally in Morocco.
In each country, drought in one or a few northern and central rainfed clusters was more strongly associated with RREs than nationally averaged drought.


Interpretation. RREs record when hydroclimatic stress becomes publicly visible and institutionally recognized. They do not measure drought or its impacts. They are an institutional climate-risk signal, positioned between environmental hazard and downstream impacts.

title: Rain Rituals and Drought Governance
text:
Scientific significance
The study offers a measurable institutional climate-risk signal for data-scarce drylands, complementing physical drought indicators. A next step is to test whether institutional recognition precedes drought-relief measures, irrigation and groundwater interventions, or agricultural land-use decisions. A related line of work concerns early-warning design in Algeria’s Drought Shield program.






In the news. When a Prayer Is Also a Climate Signal. Eos (AGU), 3 December 2025, by Nathaniel Scharping. doi:10.1029/2025EO250450

title: Data Centers & Environmental Risk
text:
Research question
What environmental risks does data-center expansion create for electricity systems, water resources, air quality and nearby communities, and how do climate extremes change them?

title: Data Centers & Environmental Risk
text:
Scientific motivation
Data centers concentrate electricity demand and cooling needs in specific places. Those places differ in water availability, grid capacity and exposure to climate extremes. Assessing these risks requires combining infrastructure information with environmental and climate data at regional and global scales.

title: Data Centers & Environmental Risk
text:
Research objectives

Assess data-center electricity demand and its implications for grid connectivity and transmission infrastructure.
Characterize water withdrawal, consumption and cooling requirements under climate variability.
Examine air-quality implications, including backup generation.
Evaluate environmental-equity dimensions of where data centers are sited.

title: Data Centers & Environmental Risk
text:
Planned approach

Integrate remote sensing and climate data with infrastructure and siting information.
Develop regional and global environmental-risk assessments using spatial, multifactor indicators.

title: Doctoral research
text:
I completed my PhD in Geographical Sciences at the University of Maryland in 2026, directed by Tatiana V. Loboda and mentored by Molly E. Brown. My dissertation, Drought and Agricultural Land-Use Change in North Africa, examined how drought shapes agricultural land use across Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia.
From the start, I wanted to put people in the equation. Satellites show where farmland changes, but not how societies experience drought. So alongside satellite and climate records, I read drought through the moment states publicly recognize it: state-organized rain rituals.
The work also meant going to the fields. Over the 2023–2024 season I drove thousands of kilometres through the cereal belt of all three countries, collecting an independent, probability-sampled ground truth to test how well satellite maps capture the region’s farmland.

title: Doctoral research
text:
Findings


01
Institutional recognition follows agricultural drought. The odds of a state-organized rain ritual rose as drought over cropland intensified. All rituals fell within the rainfed cropping season, and drought in northern and central rainfed clusters was more strongly associated with them than nationally averaged drought. Rituals mark institutional recognition; they do not measure drought impacts.
Accepted · Environmental Research: Climate


02
Fallow is where satellite maps disagree. Design-based estimates put cropland at 7.015 Mha in Morocco, 6.786 Mha in Algeria and 2.028 Mha in Tunisia. Fallow, 31.7% of cropland, was where disagreement among the three satellite products concentrated. Adding woody agriculture to the definition reversed the direction of one product’s area difference in all three countries.
Manuscript in preparation


03
When drought strikes matters most. Persistent cropland change occurred in 61.3% of grid cells (2000–2024): mostly expansion in Algeria, mostly contraction in Morocco and Tunisia. Drought characteristics accounted for 47–57% of out-of-fold spatial variation in change rates, and seasonal timing carried the most information. These are predictive associations, not causal attribution.
Manuscript in preparation



Why it matters. Better drought governance starts with what people experience on the ground. Early warning in drylands should track when and where drought strikes, not only how severe it is on average. It should pair satellite indicators with signals of how communities and institutions recognize drought, and it needs cropland maps built on consistent definitions and independent field data. The dissertation and its field dataset give agencies and researchers a practical basis for all three.

title: About
text:
Walid Ouaret is an Earth observation scientist and a Postdoctoral Fellow at The Earth Commons Institute, Georgetown University, where he works with Roshanak (Roshi) Nateghi in the SuRGE Lab. His research examines how climate extremes affect agricultural landscapes, critical infrastructure and the institutions that manage environmental risk.
He received his Ph.D. in Geographical Sciences from the University of Maryland, College Park in 2026. His dissertation, Drought and Agricultural Land-Use Change in North Africa, was directed by Tatiana V. Loboda, with mentorship from Molly E. Brown. It combined a probability-based field survey across Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia, satellite cropland records and an archival record of state-organized rain rituals.
Before his doctorate, he worked on landscape and agricultural modeling at INRAE (Montpellier and Paris) and at Wageningen University, and on remote sensing and GIS research at Miami University’s Geospatial Analysis Center. He trained as an agronomist at the École Nationale Supérieure Agronomique in Algiers. He holds master’s degrees from Paris-Saclay University and AgroParisTech, and from the Mediterranean Agronomic Institute of Chania. He co-developed the NASA-funded Open Climate Science for Agriculture curriculum, taught in English, French and Arabic.

title: Drought and Long-Term Cropland Change Across North Africa
text: Completed · manuscript in preparation

title: Drought and Long-Term Cropland Change Across North Africa
text:
Research question
Which characteristics of drought (frequency, severity, persistence or seasonal timing) are most closely associated with persistent cropland expansion and contraction in North Africa?

title: Drought and Long-Term Cropland Change Across North Africa
text:
Scientific motivation
Most climate–agriculture research focuses on crop yield or production. Yet drought can also change whether land is planted, kept in cultivation, left fallow or withdrawn from cropping. The effects of drought on the long-term spatial extent of cultivation in North Africa remain poorly understood.

title: Drought and Long-Term Cropland Change Across North Africa
text:
Geographic scope
Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia, 2000–2024, analysed on a 0.05° grid (cells of roughly 5 × 5 km).

title: Drought and Long-Term Cropland Change Across North Africa
text:
Data and methods

Cropland change. Annual 30 m cropland observations from GACED30 were aggregated to 0.05° cells. Trends were estimated with the Theil–Sen estimator, and change was treated as persistent where the 95% confidence interval excluded zero.
Drought. Monthly SPEI-1, with a drought month defined as SPEI-1 ≤ −0.5. Drought was characterized along four dimensions: frequency and exposure, severity and intensity, duration and persistence, and seasonal timing (three-month windows of the September–August agricultural year).
Models. Country-specific random forest regression evaluated by repeated 10-fold cross-validation, with leave-one-dimension-out analysis, held-out permutation importance and spatially blocked classification. Comparison of 2000–2014 with 2015–2024.

title: Drought and Long-Term Cropland Change Across North Africa
text:
Principal findings

Persistent change. Persistent change occurred in 6,799 of 11,100 cells (61.3%). Expansion made up 61.3% of significantly changing cells in Algeria. Contraction made up 90.3% in Morocco and 63.4% in Tunisia.
Association with drought. Drought characteristics accounted for 47–57% of out-of-fold spatial variation in cropland-change rates (cross-validated R² 0.473, 0.516 and 0.573 in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia).
Seasonal timing. Timing was the most informative dimension everywhere. Removing it lowered R² by 0.222, 0.174 and 0.153, against at most 0.018 for any other dimension. The most informative season differed: early season in Algeria, early and mid-season in Morocco, late and hot-dry seasons in Tunisia.
Direction of change. Drought characteristics separated contraction from expansion more clearly in Algeria (AUC 0.820) and Tunisia (AUC 0.845) than in Morocco (AUC 0.665).
Later period. After 2015, median change rates moved toward contraction in Algeria and Morocco. Drought characteristics did not explain the later trajectories consistently better, which is consistent with water access, investment and other factors shaping post-2015 change.


Interpretation. These are predictive associations. Model performance should not be read as a causal estimate of the share of agricultural change attributable to drought. Irrigation, groundwater access, policy and socioeconomic conditions were not modeled directly.

title: Drought and Long-Term Cropland Change Across North Africa
text:
Scientific significance
The relationship between drought and cropland change depends on when drought occurs within the agricultural year and on the crops and water systems exposed to it. Drought monitoring for agriculture therefore benefits from seasonally and spatially resolved indicators, rather than whole-period summaries alone.

title: Climate & Energy Infrastructure Resilience
text: Proposed research

title: Climate & Energy Infrastructure Resilience
text:
Research question
How does drought create vulnerability in electricity systems, and how can geospatial evidence and AI-assisted analysis support resilience decisions for energy infrastructure?

title: Climate & Energy Infrastructure Resilience
text:
Scientific motivation
Drought affects energy systems through water availability, cooling and generation, and these effects interact with other climate hazards. My doctoral work showed that when and where drought occurs matters for agricultural outcomes. This direction asks whether timing- and location-aware drought indicators can similarly inform the exposure and resilience of critical infrastructure.

title: Climate & Energy Infrastructure Resilience
text:
Research objectives

Characterize drought-related vulnerability of electricity systems.
Examine climate–power-grid interactions and the exposure of energy infrastructure to multiple hazards.
Develop geospatial indicators of infrastructure vulnerability.
DROUGHT-GRID, a proposed research framework: evaluate how AI-assisted analysis can support energy-resilience decisions under drought.

title: Climate & Energy Infrastructure Resilience
text:
Planned approach

Integrate Earth observation and climate records with infrastructure location and exposure information.
Apply multi-hazard, spatially explicit risk-assessment methods.
Evaluate AI-assisted analyses against transparent, reproducible baselines.

title: SEEDS: Satellite-Enabled Earth Observation & Digital Solutions for Agriculture
text:
Role: Project Lead · Funding: 6th Grain · Period: 2025–2026
SEEDS puts satellite Earth observation and digital tools to work for agricultural decision-making. From October 14 to 17, 2025, the project ran the SEEDS Seminar Series: four days of talks on remote sensing and AI for agriculture and food security. It was held online and hosted by the Department of Geographical Sciences, University of Maryland. Speakers came from NASA Harvest, NASA Acres, Harvard and the University of Montana.
